analysis.one_liner: Caps yearly out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $2,000 per person, $4,000 per family.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in three House committees since its April 2025 introduction, with no committee vote and no floor vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes a yearly dollar cap on what people pay out of pocket for prescription drugs into federal law: $2,000 per person and $4,000 per family, rising each year with medical inflation. It applies to plans sold on the ACA marketplaces and, through parallel amendments to existing law, to employer-sponsored and group health plans. Today, people with serious conditions like cancer or diabetes can face thousands of dollars in drug cost-sharing on top of their deductibles; this bill would set a hard ceiling on that amount starting in 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured people who use expensive prescription drugs. The cap protects anyone whose yearly drug copays, coinsurance, or deductible charges would otherwise exceed the limit, which hits people with chronic and serious illnesses hardest. The cap rises each year with medical inflation rather than being fixed forever.

how_it_helps.text: Caps prescription drug cost-sharing under ACA marketplace plans at $2,000 per individual and $4,000 per family per year, starting with plan years in 2026 [S2]
Applies the same cap to employer group plans by amending the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code, so the protection is not limited to marketplace coverage [S2]
Increases the cap each year after 2026 by the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index, so the ceiling tracks medical inflation rather than eroding [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that fund health plans bear the additional drug costs above the cap, and they may pass some of that through as higher premiums to all enrollees. The bill does not directly cap what drug manufacturers charge.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers and employers funding drug benefits

drawbacks.text: The cap applies only to drugs the plan actually covers; a plan could respond by covering fewer drugs or placing more drugs on tiers with restrictions, since insurers can redesign formularies to manage their new cost exposure [S2]
Costs absorbed by insurers and employers do not disappear; plans may offset them by raising premiums for everyone, including people who use no prescription drugs [S2]
A $2,000 per-person cap is still a large annual amount for many households, and people without insurance get no protection from this bill [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with serious illnesses, a hard ceiling on yearly drug cost-sharing is a substantial, concrete protection — it converts an open-ended exposure into a known maximum. The honest cost is that someone pays the difference: insurers and employers will likely offset it through premiums or tighter drug coverage rules, spreading the cost across all enrollees. The bill leaves drug prices themselves untouched, so it treats the symptom (what patients pay at the counter) rather than the cause (what drugs cost).

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2025 and sent to three House committees, and none of them has acted on it — no committee vote, no floor vote, and the House has not taken it up since referral.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Horsford introduced the Capping Prescription Costs Act of 2025 in the House on April 1, 2025, joined by nine colleagues [S1]
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means Committees [S4]
No further action appears in the bill's history after the referral; no committee has reported it and the House has not voted on it [S4]

The bill's text would cap prescription drug cost-sharing at $2,000 per person and $4,000 per family for plan years beginning in 2026, with inflation indexing thereafter, across marketplace and group health plans [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so the people better off under the current state of play are insurers and employers that fund prescription benefits, which keep the ability to shift drug costs onto patients through cost-sharing. For patients, the protection exists only on paper and has not moved toward becoming law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers keeping cost-shifting flexibility

for.name: Rep. Steven Horsford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 1, 2025 and put forward the $2,000/$4,000 drug cost-sharing cap.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors are House Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored, and the bill has received no votes that would show a partisan split.

industries.note: The cap forces insurers to cover drug cost-sharing above $2,000/$4,000 instead of passing it to patients, a real cost to them; they can offset it by raising premiums or restricting which drugs are covered. Insurers profit from cost-sharing designs that shift expenses onto sick customers, so their interest here runs against the patients the cap protects.

Employers that self-fund or sponsor group plans bear a share of the new cost above the cap. Large employers have already absorbed a similar $2,000 cap for Medicare-style costs in other contexts, but some may trim benefits or raise employee premium contributions.

When patients' out-of-pocket costs are capped, they are more likely to fill expensive prescriptions, which sustains drug sales. The bill does nothing to lower drug prices themselves, so manufacturers keep their pricing power.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic cosponsors, a three-committee referral, and no committee action more than half a year into the session, the bill is very likely to die quietly at the end of this Congress without ever getting a vote — the usual fate for a House health bill that no committee chair schedules for markup.
